content: A dysplastic nevus is an atypical mole that differs in appearance from common moles. These nevi are generally larger than ordinary moles and have irregular, indistinct borders. Their coloration is often non-uniform, ranging from pink to dark brown. While they are usually flat, some parts may be raised above the skin surface. Dysplastic nevi can appear anywhere on the body but are most commonly found on the trunk in men and on the calves in women. Dysplastic nevi are classified as a type of melanocytic lesion. Depending on the degree of cytologic atypia, melanocytic lesions can range from dysplastic nevi to melanoma. It is essential to differentiate dysplastic nevi from common moles and melanoma during diagnosis. Epidemiologically, dysplastic nevi are more commonly observed in males than in females. The most significant risk factor for the development of dysplastic nevi is exposure to sunlight. Patients with dysplastic nevi should undergo regular screening to monitor for potential progression to melanoma. If left untreated, dysplastic nevi can progress to melanoma. Complications associated with dysplastic nevi include the development of melanoma and subsequent metastasis. The definitive diagnosis of a dysplastic nevus requires tissue removal and histopathological examination to confirm dysplasia. When an atypical mole is identified, a biopsy is performed to achieve an accurate diagnosis. Local anesthetic is used to numb the area, and the mole is excised for biopsy. The tissue sample is then sent to a laboratory, where a pathologist evaluates it. Surgical excision is the primary treatment for dysplastic nevi. To prevent the development of dysplastic nevi, individuals should protect their skin from sun exposure and avoid the use of sunlamps and tanning booths. For those with dysplastic nevi, it is particularly critical to avoid sunburns and suntans to minimize the risk of progression to melanoma.
